757.title: Uppalavanna
757.hook: foremost in psychic power among the nuns, and a survivor of terrible harm, told with care
757.howItsDone: In the Theravada tradition, Khema and Uppalavanna are remembered together as the Buddha's chief women disciples, and the story of Uppalavanna's forest hut is told as the reason nuns were given a dwelling in town.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abyakata: Khema answered King Pasenadi, and later the Buddha gave him the same answer. Your line: the same answer. Did you thank a quiet teacher? Today, another of the women. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

Two names. In a short passage of the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha names two nuns as the measure for his nuns: a nun of faith, it says, may hope to become like Khema and like Uppalavanna. Khema we met yesterday, the wise one. Today is the other. Uppalavanna's name, tradition says, comes from the blue lotus, the color of her skin. The texts remember her for power. The commentaries also remember a harm done to her that no one should ever suffer. Today's story touches it once, gently, and spends longer on who she was before it and after it. Her life is not the harm.
screen: `TWO NUNS AS THE MEASURE.` → `NAMED FOR THE BLUE LOTUS.` → `HER LIFE IS NOT THE HARM.`

segments.voice: First, who she is. In the list of foremost disciples, Uppalavanna is named first among the nuns for psychic power, the power the texts call iddhi. That's her title, and it comes from the Buddha. Second, the harm, told the way the Dhammapada commentary tells it, and no further. She was living alone in a hut in the forest. A man who had long wanted her hid there and forced himself on her. She was already awakened, the story says. The deed was his, and the story treats it as his alone. Tradition says the earth opened and took him. Third, what came after. Some monks wondered aloud whether an awakened person might still take pleasure in such things. The Buddha answered that one who is awakened clings to sense pleasures no more than water clings to a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed to the point of a needle. She was not stained. And something practical changed too: tradition says that afterward the Buddha asked that nuns not live alone in the forest, and King Pasenadi had a dwelling built for them inside the town. Fourth, her own voice. In the Connected Discourses, Mara, the tempter, finds her standing alone at the foot of a sal tree in full flower, and asks whether she isn't afraid of rogues. She answers that she is not. She has mastered her mind, she says, and he can't frighten her. That's the Uppalavanna the texts keep: not only what was done to her, but who she was before it and after it. She survived.
screen: `FOREMOST IN POWER.` · `A HARM, AND IT WAS HIS.` · `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` · `MARA FINDS HER UNAFRAID.` · then, large: `SHE SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a survivor. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who came through something hard that was not their fault. You don't need the details; those are theirs. Just hold the whole person in mind: their laugh, their skill, the way they are now. If wishing them well comes easily, let it come. If this brushes against something of your own, it's enough to keep breathing, slowly, and let the breath be steady. The bell holds the time.
Uppalavanna. The nun named foremost in psychic power, who survived harm that was never hers, and met Mara unafraid. Today's word.

Your line: she survived. Today, when someone's hard story comes up, in a conversation or the news, look for the person beyond the harm, and name one thing about them that isn't the wound. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Patacara the teacher
758.hook: the woman who lost everything becomes a teacher of other grieving women
758.howItsDone: Patacara's verses and the verses of the women she taught are read in the Therigatha, and in Theravada communities her story is told as a teaching on grief and on how short and uncertain life is.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uppalavanna, foremost in psychic power, who met Mara unafraid. Your line: she survived. Whose story did you see whole? Today, a survivor who turned around and taught. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

An arrow, lodged where nobody can see it. That's how a group of grieving mothers, in the verses of the elder nuns, speak of their sorrow for their children. And they name the woman who drew it out: Patacara. Her own losses are the part of her story tradition tells first: a husband, children, parents, all lost, tradition says, in a stretch of days so terrible that she wandered out of her mind with grief, until she reached the Buddha. That's usually where the telling stops. Today it keeps going. The woman who lost everything becomes the one other grieving women come looking for.
screen: `AN ARROW NO ONE CAN SEE.` → `SHE DREW IT OUT.` → `THE GRIEVING COME TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, her own waking. In her verses in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Patacara tells how she washed her feet and watched the water as it ran down the slope, and steadied her mind on it. The commentary adds what she saw: some water went a little way, some further, some further still, the way lives run short and long. That evening she took a lamp into her cell, sat on her bed, and drew down the wick with a needle. As the flame went out, her mind was freed. Second, what she says to the grieving. In another poem, grieving mothers remember what she told them. You don't know the way he came, she says, or the way he went. He came from somewhere unseen and went on somewhere unseen. So why weep, crying, my son? It sounds hard on paper. In the poem it lands as the voice of someone who stood in the same place. Third, what the women say back. In the verses, they tell how she drew out the arrow from their hearts, the grief for their children, and they go forth as nuns. Other nuns' verses name her too: they did as Patacara taught, washed their feet, went to their cells, and woke. Fourth, the title. In the list of foremost disciples, Patacara is named first among the nuns who know the discipline, the community's rules. The woman who once wandered wild with grief became the keeper of order. Grief didn't vanish. It became a way to recognize someone else's. From grief to teacher.
screen: `WATER DOWN A SLOPE, A LAMP GOES OUT.` · `HE CAME AND WENT UNSEEN.` · `SHE DREW OUT THE ARROW.` · `KEEPER OF THE DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FROM GRIEF TO TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help one person in grief. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is grieving now: a loss this year, or an old one that still sits close. Patacara didn't lead with answers. She sat down with people first. So just hold this person in mind, and ask what might actually help. A message. A meal. Their person's name, said out loud. Your company, with nothing to fix. Choose one thing, small and doable. Then let it rest, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Salla, a dart or arrow. What grieving women say Patacara drew out of their hearts, the grief for their children. Today's word.
Your line: from grief to teacher. Today, do the one small thing you chose for someone who is grieving, and keep it simple. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

759.title: Dhammadinna
759.hook: foremost among nuns in teaching; the Buddha says he would have answered as she did (MN 44)
759.howItsDone: The Culavedalla Sutta, Dhammadinna's dialogue with Visakha, is studied in Theravada monasteries and Buddhist study groups as a short, careful teaching on identity, the path and feeling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salla: Patacara, who woke as a lamp went out and became a teacher of the grieving. Your line: from grief to teacher. Did you do your one small thing? Today, a nun whose answers the Buddha stood behind. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A man goes to see a nun, and he brings questions. His name is Visakha, a lay follower, and he isn't a stranger to the nun he's come to see: the commentaries say she had been his wife, before she went forth. Her name is Dhammadinna. He sits down to one side and starts asking. What is identity? Where does it come from? What's the path that ends it? She answers each one, cleanly. And he keeps going, question after question, until he goes one question too far. This Visakha, by the way, is a man. The laywoman Visakha comes in a few days.
screen: `A MAN WITH QUESTIONS.` → `HIS FORMER WIFE, NOW A NUN.` → `ONE QUESTION TOO FAR.`

segments.voice: First, the questions, from the forty-fourth discourse of the Middle Length collection. They aren't easy. Visakha asks what identity is, and she answers that the teaching calls it the five aggregates people cling to: body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. He asks about the noble eightfold path, about meditation, about pleasant and painful feeling and what tendency lies underneath each one. Her answers are short and exact. Second, the edge. At last he asks: what is the counterpart of nibbana? And she stops him. Friend Visakha, she says, you've gone too far; you couldn't find the limit of your questions. The holy life is grounded in nibbana, it ends in nibbana. If you wish, go and ask the Buddha, and remember what he tells you. Third, the endorsement. Visakha goes. He tells the Buddha the whole conversation. And the Buddha says: Dhammadinna is wise, of great wisdom. If you had asked me, I would have answered exactly as she did. That is the meaning, and so you should remember it. Fourth, her title. In the list of foremost disciples, Dhammadinna is named first among the nuns who teach the Dhamma. Notice the echo. Three days ago, Khema answered a king, and the Buddha's answer matched hers. Today, Dhammadinna answers Visakha, and again the Buddha says: the same. The texts make the point twice, on purpose or not: a woman taught, and the teaching stood. She taught him.
screen: `HE ASKS, SHE ANSWERS.` · `"YOU'VE GONE TOO FAR, FRIEND."` · `"I WOULD HAVE ANSWERED THE SAME."` · `FOREMOST AMONG NUNS WHO TEACH.` · then, large: `SHE TAUGHT HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a teacher you learned from. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who taught you something that held up, and who also knew where to stop: who said, that's enough for today, or, go and ask someone who knows more. A teacher, a coach, a grandparent, a coworker who showed you how it's actually done. What did they teach you? Put it into one plain sentence, silently. Hold their face in mind for a moment, and let thanks come if it comes. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhammadinna. The nun named foremost in teaching, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself. Today's word.
Your line: she taught him. Today, credit one person by name for something they taught you, to their face or to someone else. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: The mustard seed, after
760.hook: Kisa Gotami becomes a nun known for rough robes and a clear mind
760.howItsDone: Kisa Gotami's mustard seed story is told by Buddhist teachers as a teaching on death and grief, and her verses and her answer to Mara are read in the Therigatha and the Connected Discourses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhammadinna, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself. Your line: she taught him. Who did you credit? Today, a story some people know, and what came after it. Day seven hundred sixty.

A young mother carries her dead child from door to door, asking for medicine. The Buddha tells her he can help, if she brings him a mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died. She knocks, and knocks. Every house has its dead. Somewhere along that street she understands, and she lays her son down. That's the mustard seed, as the commentaries tell it. But Kisa Gotami's story doesn't end on that street. She goes forth as a nun. And the texts remember her for two things that sound small: rough robes, and a mind that couldn't be shaken.
screen: `A SEED FROM A HOUSE WITHOUT DEATH.` → `EVERY HOUSE HAS ITS DEAD.` → `THE STORY KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, where we left her. In the commentary's telling, she lays her child down in the charnel ground and goes back to the Buddha. Did you get the mustard seed? She says she's done with the seed; she has seen that death touches every house. And she asks to go forth. Second, the robes. In the list of foremost disciples, Kisa Gotami is named first among the nuns who wear rough robes. Rough robes, tradition says, means coarse cloth, cast-off pieces gathered from rubbish heaps and charnel grounds, washed, dyed and stitched. She chose plain cloth. Not poverty for show. A life with less to guard. Third, the clear mind. In the Connected Discourses, Mara, the tempter, finds her sitting alone and needles her. Why sit by yourself with a tearful face, like a woman who has lost her son? Are you out here looking for a man? It's a cruel line, aimed straight at the old wound. Her answer is calm. She says she has gone past the death of sons, and with that, the search for men has ended too. She doesn't sorrow, she doesn't weep, and she isn't afraid of him. Mara, seeing she knows him, vanishes. Fourth, the thread between the two. The mother who once couldn't put her child down learned to hold everything more lightly: cloth, comfort, even sorrow. Her verses in the Therigatha tell of the deathless path she found. After the seed came a long, plain life, and a mind the tempter couldn't move.
screen: `SHE'S DONE WITH THE SEED.` · `FOREMOST IN ROUGH ROBES.` · `MARA AIMS AT THE OLD WOUND.` · `PLAIN CLOTH, CLEAR MIND.` · then, large: `AFTER THE SEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look after something plain. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one plain thing you use every day: a mug, a coat, a pair of shoes, a chair, a pen. Something nobody would ever notice. See it clearly. Where has it been with you? What has it carried, held or kept warm? If it's within reach, you might rest a hand on it. Kisa Gotami's robe was rag cloth, and she wore it with care. Let this plain thing be enough for a minute. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kisa Gotami. The mother who searched for a mustard seed from a house where no one had died, and instead found the plain truth of loss. Today's word.
Your line: after the seed. Today, mend, clean or care for one plain thing you own, instead of replacing it. Day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: Sona's ten children
761.hook: a mother of ten, left alone in old age, goes forth and awakens
761.howItsDone: Sona's verses are read in the Therigatha, and in the Theravada tradition she is remembered by her title, foremost among nuns in energy, together with the story of her late start.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami after the mustard seed: rough robes, and a mind Mara couldn't shake. Your line: after the seed. What plain thing did you care for? Today, a mother who began late. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

Her poem opens with a number. Ten children, she says, I bore from this body. Her name is Sona. The commentary fills in the rest. Her husband leaves home for the homeless life, and she divides the family wealth among her children, keeping nothing back. Once there's nothing more to hand out, the children stop caring for her. She is old now, and weak, and alone in the house she filled. So, old and worn out, with nothing left to give away, she goes to the nuns and asks to begin.
screen: `TEN CHILDREN, ONE BODY.` → `SHE GIVES IT ALL AWAY.` → `OLD, ALONE, AND SHE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, her own verses, in the Therigatha. Sona says that after bearing her children, weak and grown old, she went to a nun. The nun taught her the aggregates, the sense bases and the elements, and she went forth. Second, the work. The commentary tells it this way: she knew she had started late, so she resolved to practice through the day and through the night, as though there were no time to spare. One day the other nuns went out and left her behind to heat the water for their baths. While the water warmed, she walked up and down, practicing walking meditation, and there, the story says, beside the fire and the pot, she woke. Third, her title. In the list of foremost disciples, Sona is named first among the nuns who put forth energy. The title goes to the old mother who started last and was left to mind the water. Fourth, what her verses say she knows. By the end of her poem, she speaks of her mind as freed and her task as done. It isn't really a story about ungrateful children; they barely appear. It's about what she did with what was left: a tired body, a late start, a pot of water to heat. She didn't wait to be young again. She began where she was. Never too late.
screen: `TEN CHILDREN, THEN A NUN.` · `SHE HEATS THE BATH WATER.` · `FOREMOST IN ENERGY.` · `SHE BEGINS WHERE SHE IS.` · then, large: `NEVER TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an elder who began late. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind an older person who started something late: learned to read or swim, went back to school, picked up a brush, took up a practice, learned a new country's language. Maybe someone in your family. Hold them in mind with respect. What did it take, to begin in front of people half their age? And if something in you has been waiting for the right age, you can let that be noticed too, just noticed. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Viriya, energy or effort. The quality Sona was named foremost in, after going forth late and practicing as though there were no time to spare. Today's word.
Your line: never too late. Today, tell an older person something you admire about what they started, or take one small step on a thing you've been calling too late. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

762.title: Ambapali's garden
762.hook: the courtesan of Vesali refuses a fortune for the Buddha's meal, gives her mango grove to the order, and later becomes a nun
762.howItsDone: Ambapali's meal and gift of her grove are read in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, and her verses on aging in the Therigatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona, the mother of ten who went forth late and was named foremost in energy, viriya. Your line: never too late. Whose late start did you honor? Today, a garden. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

Chariots on the road outside Vesali, going fast. In one of them rides Ambapali, the courtesan of Vesali. She has just heard that the Buddha is staying in her own mango grove, so she drove out, sat with him, and asked him to eat at her house tomorrow. He accepted, by staying silent. Now, heading home, she meets the chariots of the Licchavi princes, the ruling families of the town, and she drives straight at them, axle to axle, wheel to wheel. What's going on, Ambapali? She tells them. The Buddha is coming to her house tomorrow. And the princes want that meal for themselves.
screen: `CHARIOTS ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE INVITED HIM FIRST.` → `THE PRINCES WANT THE MEAL.`

segments.voice: First, the offer. In the Great Discourse on the Buddha's final journey, the princes ask her to give up the meal to them, and offer her a great sum of money. She refuses. Even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, she says, I wouldn't give up this meal. The princes snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman! Second, the Buddha. The princes ride on to the grove and invite him themselves. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. Her invitation came first, so it stands, even against the princes'. Third, the gift. The next day she serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands. When the meal is done, she sits to one side and gives the mango grove to the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head. He accepts it. Fourth, later. Tradition says Ambapali herself went forth as a nun. Her verses in the Therigatha look back at her own beauty, part by part, her hair, her eyes, her voice, her hands, and how age changed each one. Verse after verse ends with the same refrain: the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise. A woman who gave away a lovely grove later let go of her own loveliness too, and wrote it down plainly. The mango grove.
screen: `SHE WON'T SELL THE MEAL.` · `HER INVITATION CAME FIRST.` · `SHE GIVES THE GROVE.` · `HER VERSES ON AGE.` · then, large: `THE MANGO GROVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something beautiful away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you own that's actually beautiful, not just something you're finished with: a book you love, a plant, a scarf, a print, something you made yourself. Ambapali didn't give leftovers. She gave her grove. Is there someone who would treasure one of your beautiful things? Hold the thought, without deciding yet. Notice what it's like to imagine handing it over. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ambapali's garden. The mango grove the courtesan of Vesali gave to the order, after refusing a fortune for the Buddha's meal. Today's word.
Your line: the mango grove. Today, give one beautiful thing to someone who'll love it, and give it whole, with no strings attached. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich woman made a donation.
what it means: a courtesan kept the Buddha's meal against the princes, gave her grove, and later wrote plainly about her own aging.

763.title: Visakha's riddles
763.hook: a later story: Visakha keeps her father's ten puzzling rules, such as "don't carry the inside fire outside"
763.howItsDone: Visakha's story is told in Theravada countries from the Dhammapada commentary, and she is remembered by the name Migaramata, 'Migara's mother', the name her father-in-law gave her.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambapali, who wouldn't sell the Buddha's meal and gave her mango grove away. Your line: the mango grove. What beautiful thing did you give? Today, riddles from a father to his daughter. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

A wedding morning. A young woman named Visakha is leaving her father's house for her husband's family in another town. Her father, Dhananjaya, takes her aside with advice, and it comes as riddles. Don't carry the inside fire outside. Don't bring the outside fire in. Give to those who give. Don't give to those who don't. Give to both. Sit happily, eat happily, sleep happily. Tend the fire. Honor the household gods. Her new father-in-law, Migara, overhears, and it makes no sense to him. No fire outside? What if the neighbors need a light? This is a later story, from the commentary on the Dhammapada. And before it's over, Visakha will be on trial.
screen: `A WEDDING MORNING.` → `ADVICE IN RIDDLES.` → `THE FATHER-IN-LAW OVERHEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the trial. Some time later, the story says, Migara turns against his daughter-in-law and wants her sent home. She asks that her case be heard by elders who came with her from her father's town, and Migara brings up the riddles as proof that she's strange. Second, the fire. Visakha explains them, one by one. The inside fire is the household's private troubles: don't carry tales of your in-laws' faults out to the neighbors. The outside fire is the neighbors' quarrels and gossip: don't bring them home. Give to those who give means lend to people who return what they borrow; don't give to those who don't means the opposite. Give to both means help poor relatives, whether or not they can ever repay. Sitting, eating and sleeping happily mean honoring the elders of the house, and tending the fire means treating them with care, the way you'd treat a flame. Honoring the household gods means caring for holy people who come to the door. Third, the turn. The elders find her blameless, and in the commentary, Migara later comes to the Buddha's teaching through her, and tradition says he honored her by calling her his mother. Fourth, what travels. Some of these riddles belong to a young wife's duties in a household of their own time. But the first one travels well. A quarrel at home grows when it's carried out and told around the neighborhood. A quarrel next door grows when it's carried in. Visakha didn't drop her father's riddles because they puzzled someone. She kept them until the day she could say what they meant. Don't carry the fire out.
screen: `ON TRIAL OVER RIDDLES.` · `SHE EXPLAINS EACH ONE.` · `FOUND BLAMELESS, CALLED MOTHER.` · `THE FIRST RIDDLE TRAVELS.` · then, large: `DON'T CARRY THE FIRE OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one family secret kindly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something about your family, your household or a close friend that isn't yours to tell. Not a secret that hides harm; that kind may need to be told to someone who can help. Just the ordinary private stuff: a quarrel, a worry, an embarrassment. Notice the pull to share it, the little spark of a good story. Then let it stay inside, warm and contained, the way a hearth fire stays in the hearth. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Visakha's riddles. A father's puzzling advice to his daughter, and her clear explanation of each riddle when she was put on trial. Today's word.

Your line: don't carry the fire out. Today, when you're tempted to air a family grievance to an outsider, keep it in, and if it needs taking anywhere, take it to the person it's about. And look back at this week: she survived, from grief to teacher, she taught him, after the seed, never too late, the mango grove, and now don't carry the fire out. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

fork.setup: you're Visakha. your father-in-law has called elders to judge you, and holds up your father's riddles as proof you're strange. what do you do?
options: apologize, and promise to forget the riddles.
explain what each riddle means.
go home to your father's house.
fork.reveal: she explains every riddle, the inside fire first, and is found blameless. tradition says Migara later called her his mother.

original.note: Pali aggi, fire: the inside fire and the outside fire of the riddles.

trapdoor: what you thought: strange rules about fire.
what it means: a father's advice in code: keep household troubles at home, and keep outside gossip out.
what a scholar hears: a later story from the Dhammapada commentary, not the suttas, in which Visakha explains each riddle and wins over her father-in-law Migara.
